result: Cdc42 depletion promotes robust cell-in-cell formation in adherent epithelial cells but not in suspension culture. This novel form of adherent entosis is observed across multiple cell lines (16HBE and MCF7) and is associated with disruption of junction maturation.
evaluation: Claims C51-C59 provide strong experimental evidence from multiple RNAi reagents showing robust knockdown (C51) and consistent induction of adherent entosis (C55-C57) across cell lines. The finding that Cdc42 depletion has no major effect on suspension entosis (C53) but promotes adherent entosis establishes a novel mechanism. Data from Figures 1a-i support these conclusions.

result: Adherent cell-in-cell formation upon Cdc42 depletion shares mechanistic features with conventional entosis, including dependence on α-catenin, ROCK-mediated myosin activation, and recruitment of autophagy/lysosomal machinery.
evaluation: Claims C60-C65 demonstrate that adherent entosis requires α-catenin (C60-C62), is suppressed by ROCK inhibition (C63), shows enriched phospho-myosin in internalizing cells (C64), and recruits LC3 and LAMP1 (C65). These findings are supported by data in Figures 1j-n and establish that adherent entosis shares core mechanistic features with conventional entosis.

result: Mitosis drives adherent entosis but not suspension entosis. During every analyzed adherent cell-in-cell event, the inner cell penetrates its host during or shortly after mitosis, and inhibition of mitosis profoundly decreases adherent but not suspension entosis.
evaluation: Claims C68-C72 are strongly supported by timelapse imaging (C68), Cdk1 inhibitor experiments showing differential effects on adherent versus suspension conditions (C69-C70), and 3D-CLEM data (Figure 2d). The conclusion that there are two mechanistically distinct routes to entosis (C71-C72) is well-justified by the experimental evidence.

result: Loss of Cdc42 specifically promotes internalization of dividing cells, while wild-type adherent cells can efficiently act as entotic hosts. Cdc42 depletion does not promote entosis by mimicking matrix deadhesion.
evaluation: Claims C73-C80 are supported by co-culture experiments showing that Cdc42-depleted cells are almost always the inner cell (C73-C74) and that wild-type cells act as hosts (C77). The observation of RFP-zyxin foci in hosts (C79-C80) and the inability of β1-integrin depletion to induce entosis (C121) support the conclusion that this is not simply mimicking deadhesion (C78).

result: Cdc42 controls mitotic morphology in polarized epithelial cells. Cdc42 depletion enhances mitotic deadhesion and rounding from prometaphase onwards, without affecting cell cycle progression. This phenotype is distinct from spindle misorientation.
evaluation: Claims C85-C95 are well-supported by flow cytometry showing no cell cycle defects (C85), live imaging demonstrating enhanced mitotic rounding and deadhesion (C92-C94), and quantitative measurements (Figure 3c-d). The control experiment with aPKC depletion (C89-C91) effectively rules out spindle misorientation as the driver of entosis.

result: Cdc42 constrains mitotic RhoA activation in polarized epithelial cells. Upon Cdc42 depletion, cortical RhoA activity is enriched at the metaphase cortex (37% of cells), accompanied by increased cortical actin.
evaluation: Claims C99-C103 are supported by FRET biosensor data showing low RhoA activity in control metaphase cells (C99) versus enriched cortical RhoA in 37% of Cdc42-depleted cells (C100), along with increased cortical actin (C101). The conclusion that Cdc42 constrains mitotic RhoA activation (C102-C103) is well-justified by Figure 4a-c data.

result: Aberrant activation of a Rho/ROCK/myosin cascade during mitosis drives enhanced retraction and rounding. Inhibition of Rho proteins, ROCK, or myosin rescues mitotic cell spreading in Cdc42-depleted cells.
evaluation: Claims C104-C111 are supported by experiments showing that C3 transferase, Y-27632 (ROCK inhibitor), and blebbistatin (myosin inhibitor) all significantly increase basal area in Cdc42-depleted mitotic cells (Figure 4d-e). The conclusion that a Rho/ROCK/myosin cascade drives enhanced rounding (C111) is well-supported.

result: Inhibition of Rap1 phenocopies Cdc42 depletion by reducing mitotic spreading, increasing rounding, and inducing adherent entosis that occurs during or shortly after mitosis and is inhibited by G2 arrest.
evaluation: Claims C113-C117 are supported by data showing DN-Rap1 reduces spreading and increases rounding (C113, Figure 5a-d), induces adherent entosis (C114), which occurs during/after mitosis (C115) and is blocked by Cdk1 inhibition (C116). This provides independent support for the model linking mitotic morphology changes to entosis (C117).

result: Simple loss of matrix attachment during interphase is insufficient to drive penetration of an adherent host. Detached interphase cells undergo efficient suspension entosis (~8%) but barely penetrate adherent hosts, establishing that mitotic biophysical changes are essential for adherent entosis.
evaluation: Claims C118-C124 are strongly supported by co-culture experiments showing detached interphase cells efficiently undergo suspension entosis but rarely penetrate adherent hosts (C118-C119, Figure 5h-i). The lack of entosis upon β1-integrin depletion (C121) further supports that matrix detachment alone is insufficient (C120). The conclusion about mechanistic differences (C123-C124) is well-justified.

result: MCF7 and HCT116 cancer cells undergo constitutive adherent entosis under basal conditions. Cell-in-cell formation is coincident with cell division and largely dependent on progression through mitosis in both 2D and 3D culture.
evaluation: Claims C125-C128 are supported by timelapse microscopy showing mitosis-coincident entosis (C126, Figure 6a-b, Videos 7-8) and Cdk1 inhibitor experiments demonstrating mitosis-dependence in both 2D and 3D (C127, Figure 6c-d). This establishes that mitotic entosis occurs constitutively in certain cancer cell lines (C128).

result: In primary human breast invasive ductal carcinomas, 31/75 tumors were positive for entosis, and among these, mitotic activity positively correlates with cell-in-cell formation with statistical significance (p<0.05).
evaluation: Claims C130-C132 are supported by tissue microarray analysis of 75 human breast ductal carcinomas showing 31 entosis-positive cases (C130) with significant positive correlation between mitotic index and cell-in-cell formation (C131, Figure 6g). The conclusion that mitosis may drive entosis in vivo (C132) is appropriately cautious given the correlative nature of the data.

result: Mitosis-induced entosis in adherent cancer cells leads to inner cell death (by apoptotic or non-apoptotic means) and host cell multinucleation, suggesting both tumor-suppressive (cell killing) and tumor-promoting (genomic instability) effects.
evaluation: Claims C133-C139 are supported by timelapse microscopy showing predominant inner cell death (C133-C134, Figure 6h-i) and quantification showing increased multinucleation in host cells versus single cells (C135-C136, Figure 6j-k). The conclusions about dual anti- and pro-tumorigenic effects (C138-C139) are appropriately stated as interpretations of the observed outcomes.

result: Taxol treatment increases mitotic index, arrests cells in prometaphase, and consistently increases cell-in-cell formation in 16HBE cells. This effect is phenocopied by nocodazole and STLC, suggesting entosis occurs as a consequence of prometaphase arrest. All three drugs significantly enhance mitotic deadhesion and rounding.
evaluation: Claims C141-C148 are well-supported by experimental data showing taxol increases mitotic index and entosis (C141-C143), with similar effects from nocodazole and STLC (C144-C145). The inference that prometaphase arrest rather than microtubule stabilization drives entosis (C146) is reasonable given the different mechanisms of action. Quantitative data showing enhanced deadhesion and rounding (C147, Figure 7d-f) support the model (C148).

result: In both cultured MCF7 cells and mouse xenograft models, 24-hour taxol treatment promotes significant increases in mitotic index and cell-in-cell formation. Since taxol inhibits suspension entosis in MCF7 cells, the mechanisms of detached versus adherent entosis are distinct.
evaluation: Claims C149-C153 are supported by data from cultured cells and xenografts showing taxol-induced increases in mitotic index and entosis (C149-C150, Figure 7g-l). The citation that taxol inhibits suspension entosis (C151) combined with the current findings supports the conclusion about distinct mechanisms (C152). The overall conclusion (C153) is well-justified.

result: There are at least two mechanistic routes to entosis: loss of matrix attachment and cell division. Both anchorage independence and unrestrained proliferation, classic hallmarks of cancer, can drive entosis.
evaluation: Claims C154 and C156 represent well-supported conclusions synthesizing the major findings of the study. The experimental evidence clearly demonstrates two distinct triggers for entosis (matrix deadhesion and mitosis), and the connection to cancer hallmarks (C155 is established knowledge) provides important context for the biological significance.

result: The majority of internalized cells die within the entotic vacuole by either non-apoptotic or apoptotic means, establishing mitotic entosis in adherent cells as a means of epithelial cell cannibalism.
evaluation: Claims C81-C82 are supported by timelapse microscopy data (Figure 2i-j) showing that most internalized cells die, consistent with suspension entosis. The conclusion that this establishes adherent mitotic entosis as cell cannibalism (C82) is justified by the observed cell death.

result: The outcome of entosis is broadly conserved whether triggered by deadhesion or mitosis, within adherent or detached host cells.
evaluation: Claim C163 is supported by data throughout the manuscript showing similar outcomes (inner cell death, host multinucleation) across different entosis triggers and conditions, as summarized in Figure 8. This represents a valid synthesis of the findings.

result: Normal epithelia may engulf and kill aberrantly dividing neighbors in a tumor-suppressive act of 'assisted suicide.' This model is based on the finding that wild-type, fully adherent cells can act as entotic hosts.
evaluation: Claims C11, C84, and C164 represent speculative models based on the finding that wild-type cells can act as hosts (C10, C77). While the experimental observation is solid, the biological interpretation about normal epithelia eliminating aberrant cells is not directly tested and remains a hypothesis requiring further validation in physiologically relevant contexts.

result: Cell division may promote cell cannibalism in the proliferative tumor environment, and one aberrant division may promote more aberrant divisions, contributing to tumor progression.
evaluation: Claims C129 and C165 represent speculative possibilities raised by the findings but not directly tested. While the correlation between mitotic index and entosis in tumors (C131) is suggestive, the causal relationships and net effects on tumor progression remain to be established through additional experiments.

result: Primordial junctions are sufficient to support entosis in suspension culture.
evaluation: Claim C54 is presented as a suggestion based on the observation that Cdc42 depletion disrupts junction maturation but doesn't affect suspension entosis (C52-C53). However, this inference is not directly tested—the study does not demonstrate that primordial junctions alone are sufficient, only that mature junctions are not required. Additional experiments would be needed to support this conclusion.

result: The findings can in part explain the increased frequency of cell-in-cell structures among higher grade, more proliferative tumors.
evaluation: Claim C158 is supported by the combination of the current findings showing mitosis drives entosis (C71, C128) and the correlation between mitotic index and entosis in breast tumors (C131), along with the established fact that mitotic index is used to stage breast cancers (C157). This represents a reasonable interpretation connecting the findings to prior observations.
